title: Algebraize a map from a scalar extension, with torsion kernel and cokernel
statement: Let $R$ and $S$ be commutative rings and $R\to S$ a flat ring map [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map]. Let $I\subseteq R$ be a finitely generated ideal such that the induced map $R/I\to S/IS$ is an isomorphism. Call an $R$-module $I$-power torsion when for every element $x$ there is an integer $n\geq0$ such that $r x=0$ for every $r\in I^n$; for an $S$-module use restriction of scalars. Let $P$ be an $R$-module and $Q$ an $S$-module; write $S\otimes_R P$ for scalar extension and $\psi_S$ for scalar extension of a linear map [def-weil-module-base-change]. For an $S$-linear map $\varphi:S\otimes_R P\to Q$ with $I$-power torsion kernel and cokernel, there exist an $R$-module $T$, an $R$-linear map $\psi:P\to T$, and an $S$-linear isomorphism $\beta:S\otimes_R T\to Q$ such that $\beta\circ\psi_S=\varphi$, and both $\ker\psi$ and $T/\operatorname{im}\psi$ are $I$-power torsion.

proof.text: (Localizing a map with $I$-power torsion kernel and cokernel.) As $I$ is finitely generated, write $I=(f_1,\dots,f_t)$. Let $T$ be an $I$-power torsion $R$-module and $f=f_i$. For $x\in T$ pick $n\ge1$ with $I^nx=0$; then $f^nx=0$ since $f^n\in I^n$, so $x/1=0$ in $T_f$ and every element $x/f^e=(1/f^e)\cdot(x/1)$ of $T_f$ is $0$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away]: $T_f=0$. Now let $h:P\to Q$ be an $R$-linear map with $I$-power torsion kernel and cokernel. Localizing the exact sequences $0\to\operatorname{Ker}h\to P\xrightarrow{h}Q$ and $P\xrightarrow{h}Q\to\operatorname{Coker}h\to0$ at $f$ gives exact sequences $(\operatorname{Ker}h)_f\to P_f\xrightarrow{h_f}Q_f$ and $P_f\xrightarrow{h_f}Q_f\to(\operatorname{Coker}h)_f$ [lem-weil-pbc-localization-module-exact] whose outer terms are $0$; so $h_f$ is injective and surjective, an isomorphism. If $h$ is $S$-linear between $S$-modules, $h_f$ is $S$-linear, because the $S$-action on $P_f$, $Q_f$ is by the localized multiplications and $h_f\circ(s\cdot)_f=(h\circ s\cdot)_f=(s\cdot\circ h)_f=(s\cdot)_f\circ h_f$. In particular, in (1) and (2), $\varphi'_{f_i}$ is an $S$-linear isomorphism for every $i$.

proof.text: (Build and algebraize the datum for a map out of a scalar extension.) Now $\varphi':M\otimes_RS\to N'$ and by step 1 $\varphi'_{f_i}$ is an $S$-linear isomorphism. Put $\mathbf D'=(N',(M_{f_i})_i,(c^M_{f_i}\circ(\varphi'_{f_i})^{-1})_i,(\sigma^M_{f_i,f_j})_{i,j})$. It is an object of $\mathrm{Glue}$ [def-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-data]: (b) is (b) for $\mathrm{Can}(M)$ [prop-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-equivalence] (1); for (a), the identity $\sigma^{N'}_{f_i,f_j}\circ(\varphi'_{f_i})_{f_j}=(\varphi'_{f_j})_{f_i}\circ\sigma^{M\otimes S}_{f_i,f_j}$ (checked on $(m/f_i^a)/f_j^b$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away]) and $((\varphi'_{f_i})^{-1})_{f_j}=((\varphi'_{f_i})_{f_j})^{-1}$ give $\sigma^{M\otimes S}_{f_i,f_j}\circ((\varphi'_{f_i})^{-1})_{f_j}=((\varphi'_{f_j})^{-1})_{f_i}\circ\sigma^{N'}_{f_i,f_j}$, To check the square, substitute $\alpha_i=c^M_{f_i}\circ(\varphi'_{f_i})^{-1}$ into its left side. Move the localized inverse past the canonical interchange by the displayed naturality identity. The square identity for $\mathrm{Can}(M)$ then replaces $(\sigma^M_{f_i,f_j}\otimes S)\circ c^{M_{f_i}}_{f_j}\circ(c^M_{f_i})_{f_j}\circ\sigma^{M\otimes S}_{f_i,f_j}{}^{-1}$ by $c^{M_{f_j}}_{f_i}\circ(c^M_{f_j})_{f_i}$; composing with the localized inverse and with $\sigma^{N'}_{f_i,f_j}$ gives exactly the right side of the required square. Equivalently, precompose the desired square with the bijective double localization of $\varphi'$: its two sides reduce by inverse cancellation and naturality to the two sides of the canonical square. This precomposition is injective on maps, so the desired square holds. $\Phi'=(\varphi',(\mathrm{id}_{M_{f_i}})_i):\mathrm{Can}(M)\to\mathbf D'$ is a morphism, since $(c^M_{f_i}\circ(\varphi'_{f_i})^{-1})\circ\varphi'_{f_i}=(\mathrm{id}\otimes_RS)\circ c^M_{f_i}$. By [prop-weil-pbc-formal-glueing-equivalence] (2) there are an $R$-module $N$ and an isomorphism $\Theta=(\theta',(\theta_i)):\mathrm{Can}(N)\to\mathbf D'$, and $\Theta^{-1}\circ\Phi'=\mathrm{Can}(\psi)$ for a unique $R$-linear $\psi:M\to N$; componentwise $\psi\otimes_RS=\theta'^{-1}\circ\varphi'$ and $\psi_{f_i}=\theta_i^{-1}$. Put $\beta=\theta':N\otimes_RS\to N'$, an $S$-linear isomorphism with $\beta\circ(\psi\otimes_RS)=\varphi'$, which is (2); again every $\psi_{f_i}$ is an isomorphism.

proof.text: Let $K=\ker\psi$ and $C=\operatorname{coker}\psi$. The preceding algebraization step makes $\psi_{f_i}$ an isomorphism for every generator $f_i$ of $I$. Exact localization of the kernel and cokernel sequences [lem-weil-pbc-localization-module-exact] therefore gives $K_{f_i}=0$ and $C_{f_i}=0$. For $x$ in either module, the fraction equality criterion [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away] gives a positive integer $e_i$ with $f_i^{e_i}x=0$. Put $e=1+\sum_i e_i$. The ideal $I^e$ is generated by monomials in the $f_i$ of total degree $e$. When the family is nonempty, such a monomial contains some $f_i$ to an exponent at least $e_i$, since otherwise its total degree is at most $\sum_i(e_i-1)<e$. It therefore annihilates $x$, and so does every element of $I^e$. When the family is empty, $I=0$ and $e=1$, hence $I^e=0$ also annihilates $x$. Thus $K$ and $C$ are $I$-power torsion.
